I'm an old farmer here in Quzhou. I've been doing wheat-maize double crop for fifty years, so I mostly do what I know works. Let me think about this year.

My 16.9 mu is already planted to wheat from last October — I planted Jimai 22, an improved variety, because that's what the seed dealer in town sells and my neighbors have had good harvests with it. For the wheat base fertilizer, I already put down two bags of compound fertilizer (15-15-15) per mu before sowing, which works out to about 7-8 kg of each nutrient. This spring when the wheat turns green and starts jointing, I'll topdress urea — about one bag (25 kg) per 3 mu, so roughly 8 kg urea per mu, which gives me maybe 4 kg more nitrogen. So wheat gets about 11-12 kg N, 7-8 kg P, 7-8 kg K per mu total. I'll irrigate from my well — once before winter (winter water), once at returning-green or jointing, and once at grain-filling. Three times is standard here. Some neighbors do four if it's dry, but water costs money and my well pump uses electricity. Pesticide — I'll spray once for aphids and once with herbicide for the weeds in spring, and maybe one more fungicide at heading if I see powdery mildew. Call it 3 applications. With Jimai 22 and normal weather, I expect 500 kg per mu, maybe 550 if the rain cooperates.

After wheat harvest in June, I put in summer maize right away — no-till direct seeding into the wheat stubble, that's what everyone does now, saves time and fuel. I use Zhengdan 958 or a similar hybrid, whatever the dealer has fresh. Maize eats more nitrogen than wheat. I put a bag of compound fertilizer (15-15-15) at sowing, then topdress urea at the big-trumpet stage — one bag per 2 mu, about 12-13 kg urea per mu, giving another 6 kg N. So around 13-14 kg N, 6 kg P, 6 kg K for maize. I irrigate once right after planting to get germination, and once at tasseling if the summer rains are weak. Two irrigations usually. Spray pesticide twice — once for corn borer, once for armyworm if they show up. Maize yield around 550 kg per mu is normal for me.

I don't want to overspend on fertilizer, but I'd rather put a bit extra than lose yield — a bad harvest hurts much more than a few extra bags of fertilizer. My kids work off-farm and help with money, so I can afford what I need, but I'm careful.
